content: We recommend reflex HCV RNA testing for individuals who have a positive HCV antibody test result. This approach serves as a critical strategy to enhance linkage to care and treatment. Reflex testing can be conducted either in a laboratory setting using a specimen already available in the laboratory or in a clinical setting through immediate specimen collection following a positive HCV antibody rapid diagnostic test (RDT). Clinic-based reflex testing involves a single clinical visit where two blood samples are collected. Initially, a capillary (fingerstick) whole blood sample is taken and tested using a rapid diagnostic HCV antibody test. If the result is positive, a second blood sample (either venous or fingerstick) is immediately collected for HCV RNA testing to confirm active infection. The second sample may be sent to a laboratory for HCV RNA NAT (or HCV antigen) testing or tested on-site using a point-of-care HCV RNA NAT assay. The advantages of reflex testing, whether laboratory-based or clinic-based, include improved outcomes across the HCV care continuum. These benefits include increased uptake of HCV RNA testing, reduced time to testing, enhanced linkage to care, and faster initiation of treatment. Reflex testing also eliminates the need for additional clinic visits, saving time, reducing inconvenience, and lowering costs. Access to point-of-care HCV RNA NAT assays can further facilitate clinic-based reflex sample collection. A systematic review and meta-analysis commissioned by WHO evaluated the impact of laboratory-based and clinic-based reflex HCV RNA testing on reducing turnaround time between HCV antibody screening and HCV RNA testing, as well as on linkage to care and treatment. The evidence suggests that reflex testing significantly reduces the time to treatment initiation compared to the standard multi-step approach. However, most studies included in the review were observational (cross-sectional or cohort studies), with no randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Many studies had a high risk of bias, and the quality of evidence was low. Turnaround time from antibody testing to reflex sample collection was reported as 0 days in most studies. However, the time from RNA testing to treatment initiation varied, ranging from 52 to 83 days in viremic cases. Delays in some studies were attributed to batch testing in laboratories with low sample volumes, requiring sufficient samples to justify running an assay. Clinic-based reflex testing has shown promise in reducing turnaround times. For example, in 13 studies, the median turnaround time from RNA sample collection to HCV RNA NAT testing was 0 days in 10 studies, 1 day in two studies, and 5 days in one study. Reflex testing also simplifies the care pathway, reducing the need for additional clinic visits and expediting linkage to care. A survey of key public and private laboratories implementing laboratory-based reflex HCV RNA testing revealed that this approach is cost-saving compared to conventional two-step testing. Savings result from fewer clinic visits and reduced clinician time. For instance, a 2013 analysis by Public Health England estimated annual savings of £166,500 from reflex RNA NAT testing due to a reduction in the number of referrals. Reflex testing also avoids the need for additional venipuncture, which is particularly beneficial for individuals with compromised veins, such as people who inject drugs. Patient preferences strongly favor same-day initial and confirmatory HCV RNA testing. In a multi-country survey, 88% of participants preferred same-day testing, with the preference rising to 96% among people who currently or formerly inject drugs. The main reasons cited were faster diagnosis confirmation and earlier treatment initiation. Additionally, 93% of respondents preferred conducting both tests at the same location for convenience and accessibility. Reflex testing strategies, whether laboratory-based or clinic-based, can promote equity in access to care, particularly for high-risk populations such as people who inject drugs, the homeless, and incarcerated individuals. These populations benefit from the convenience of a single sample collection approach, which reduces the risk of loss to follow-up. The feasibility of implementing reflex testing has been demonstrated in various settings, particularly in high-income countries. Reflex testing simplifies the care pathway, reduces clinic visits, and accelerates linkage to care. Countries should incorporate routine reflex HCV RNA testing into their national testing guidelines and infrastructure. The choice between laboratory-based and clinic-based reflex testing will depend on factors such as national policies, budgets, infrastructure, and the availability of centralized laboratories and sample transport networks. For populations with limited access to laboratory services, clinic-based reflex testing with point-of-care HCV RNA testing may maximize linkage to care. A mixed approach combining laboratory-based and clinic-based reflex testing may be optimal to address the needs of different populations and regions. To implement laboratory-based reflex HCV RNA testing, key steps include training phlebotomy and laboratory staff, updating electronic laboratory order forms, designing processes to preserve specimen integrity, and planning for additional costs. Combining laboratory-based reflex testing with other strategies, such as clinic-based reflex testing, can address diverse population needs. Regular evaluation of reflex testing programs is essential for quality improvement. A case study from Vall d’Hebron Clinical Laboratories in Barcelona, Spain, highlights the impact of reflex testing. Previously, only 52% of positive HCV antibody tests led to viral load testing, with even lower rates in drug addiction care centers. The conventional testing strategy required five visits over at least four weeks to confirm a diagnosis. In March 2018, Vall d’Hebron implemented a one-step reflex testing process, reducing the time to diagnosis from four weeks to two days. Results of HCV RNA testing were provided within 24 hours for tests conducted Monday through Thursday and within three days for tests conducted on Friday. This streamlined approach significantly improved the efficiency of HCV diagnosis and care.
